blocks.text: It is proved that קאת kaath is the pelican and the heron, especially the starred heron, that is, the bittern.

For the Greeks, here and in the seventh verse of Psalm 101 (102 for the Hebrews), קאת kaath is the pelican. So too for Jerome in the passage of the Psalm, although elsewhere he renders it onocrotalus. Onkelos and the Samaritan retain the Hebrew word. In its place Jonathan and the Syriac have ܩܩܐ kaka; Erpenianus has القوق [al-qūq] alkuk, and the other القيق [al-qīq] alkik. Nor do the Talmudic writers say otherwise. Thus the Babylonian Talmud, tractate Cholin, ch. 3, fol. 63a: אמר רב יהודה קאת זו הקוק, R. Judah said: Kaath is kuk. So also R. Ishmael in the Jerusalem Talmud. And for קוק kuk some write קיק kik. Accordingly, in the tractate On the Sabbath, ch. 2, fol. 21a, Rabbi Samuel, asked where שמן קיק, oil of kik, comes from, answers thus: שאלתי נהו לכל נחותי ימא ואמרו לי עוף אחד יש בכרכי הים וקיק שמו, I asked this very thing of all those who go down to the sea, and they told me that a bird named kik is found in the coastal towns. And Kimchi in his Lexicon cites the passages of the Talmud as if he had read kik everywhere. His words are: ובתלמוד אמר רב יהודה קאת זה הקיק ובתלמוד ירושלמי תני רבי ישמעאל קאת זה הקיק, And in the Talmud Rabbi Judah said that kaath is kik. Also in the Jerusalem Talmud Rabbi Ishmael taught that kaath is kik. We have noted that the Arabic paraphrasts also write it both ways. Yet among them قوق [qūq] kuk and قيق [qīq] kik differ greatly. For قوق [qūq] kuk is طاير ماي طويل العنق [ṭāyir māʾī ṭawīl al-ʿunuq], a water bird with a long neck. So Alcamus and Damir define it, from the book entitled العباب [al-ʿUbāb] Alobab, that is, The Universe. But القيق [al-qīq] alkik is the crow. Damir describes it thus: القيق طاير علي قدر اليمامة واهل الشام يسمونه ابو زريق وهو الوف للناس فيه قبول للتعليم وسرعة ادراك لما يعلم ويحاكي كلما يسمع وقد تقدم الكلام [col. 293] عليه في باب الزاي المعجمة [al-qīq ṭāyir ʿalī qadr al-yamāma wa-ahl al-Shām yusammūnahu abū zurayq wa-huwa alūf li-l-nās fīhi qabūl li-l-taʿlīm wa-surʿat idrāk li-mā yuʿallam wa-yuḥākī kullamā yasmaʿ wa-qad taqaddama al-kalām ʿalayhi fī bāb al-zāy al-muʿjama] Alkik is a bird approaching the size of a turtledove, which is called by the inhabitants of Syria abu-zarik (that is, the grey-blue father). It lives with people. It has a capacity for learning and ease in grasping what it is taught. And it repeats whatever it hears. But it has already been dealt with in the chapter on Ze. That is, under the word زاغ [zāgh] Zag, which is the common name of the crow, although others explain it as the magpie ^{(1)} Since, then, the bird [III, 41] named קיק kik differs so from the bird קוק kuk, they ought not to have been confused ^{(2)}.
